> 天之道，其猶張弓與？

Chapter 76 said 強 is a bow drawn full, and full draw breaks. Chapter 77 uses the bow again — but for the other action.

## 張 is to string the bow, not to draw it

張: 施弓弦也 — to put the string onto the bow.

Not pulling. Fitting.

And stringing is a calibration: too tight and the bow is damaged though it shoots far; too loose and nothing leaves it at all. The person stringing is looking for the just-enough.

So the two chapters are the bow's two procedures: 76 is drawing, which is applying force; 77 is stringing, which is finding level. Drawing breaks; leveling lasts.

## 抑 is one hand pressing down; 舉 is two hands lifting

抑: 按也, from 手 — one hand pressing down.
舉: 對舉也, from 手 — two hands facing each other, raising.

One hand is enough to press down. Lifting takes two.

So 高者抑之，下者舉之 is not symmetrical in effort: the way of heaven spends most of its force on the lifting.

Which is the chapter's quiet observation about redistribution: taking down is easy, bringing up is expensive.

## 損 is to remove by hand; 補 is to mend a garment

損: 減也, from 手 — taken away by hand.
補: 完衣也, from 衣 — to make a torn garment whole.

So 損有餘而補不足 is not "balance the accounts." It is: take from the surplus, and mend what has worn through.

補 is repair, not topping-up. The image is cloth with a hole in it, and thread put through it.

## 人之道則不然

The human way is the opposite: 損不足以奉有餘 — take from what is short, and present it to what is already full.

The line is not a moral complaint. It is a description of a mechanism that runs by itself: the full is visible, the short is not, and offering to the visible is what a system does without being told.

## 孰能有餘以奉天下？唯有道者

Who can take the surplus and give it to the world? Only the one with the way.

The question is genuine, because the answer is not a policy. The human way is an emergent behavior; the only thing that reverses it is a person in whom the reversal has already happened.

## 為而不恃，功成而不處，其不欲見賢

Act and do not lean on it; complete and do not occupy the position; he does not want his worth to be seen.

見 is to make visible. 賢, as in chapter 75, is a price, from 貝.

So the last line closes the circle: the one who redistributes does not want the redistribution to be visible as his worth — because the moment it is, it has become the human way again, done with an account.

## A test

Take a redistribution you have done — time, money, credit, attention. Ask whether it was mending a worn place, or presenting to a place already full. The second is usually where the visibility is.
